column4: This verse’s own contribution is that God saves Noah and his family from great distress; the same passage leaves a mention for Noah in 37:78 and greets him in 37:79. It brings relief from distress together with a lasting prophetic name, as the section does with the removed burden and raised remembrance.

The section treats a raised name as lasting renown; here God says He leaves Noah remembered among later generations. The next verse’s peace upon Noah shows what that continuing mention looks like, while this ayah supplies the legacy claim itself.

The section cites Abraham’s prayer for a truthful name among later generations; here the Quran says God left Abraham a mention among later people. The following verse’s greeting of peace on Abraham gives that renown a form of praise.

The section links elevated remembrance to prophetic honor; this verse says God left Moses and Aaron a mention among later generations. The next verse’s peace upon both is the passage’s explicit honoring response.

The section’s raised-name image is repeated for Elijah: this verse says God left him a mention among later generations, and the next verse greets him with peace. Its own contribution is the continuing legacy claim.

The section’s secondary gloss for ظ ه ر describes a fault that does not attach to the innocent; this verse says one who casts a sin onto an innocent person bears slander and clear wrongdoing himself. It specifies where the blame and burden actually remain.

The section’s root و ض ع describes setting a burden down; at the Hour, this verse says every pregnant woman puts down her pregnancy. The shared bodily act makes the burden’s release concrete, though the verse’s scene is the terror of Judgment.

The section pictures a weight so heavy it strains the Prophet’s back; this verse describes Qarun’s keys as heavy enough to burden a band of strong men. It supplies a literal load whose weight is visible through those trying to carry it.

The section’s burden is removed from a person; at the final shaking, this verse says the earth casts out its loads. It transfers the image to the earth itself and makes discharged weight an end-time scene.

The section joins an opened chest with the root ذ ك ر as remembrance and honor; this verse says hearts find rest through remembrance of God. It connects remembrance to an easing of the inner state, while using remembrance devotionally rather than as public renown.

The section’s opened chest presents inward capacity as a divine gift; this verse says it is hearts within chests that can become blind. That specific inward obstruction contrasts with the section’s opened capacity and grounds the image in perception.

The section’s root ر ف ع includes literal raising as well as honor; Abraham and Ishmael raise the foundations of the House. This is a concrete physical use of the verb by Abraham, whose lasting name the section also discusses.

The section defines elevation as honor and its opposite as humiliation; this verse answers a boast that the more honored would expel the more humble by stating that honor belongs to God, His Messenger, and believers. It places the Prophet’s honor under God’s grant rather than human status claims.

This verse reports a person reading abundant provision as proof that God has honored him; the next two verses give the opposite reading and reject the inference. Its own contribution is the first mistaken equation of provision with honor, a useful boundary for the section’s raised-name image.

This verse reports a person reading restricted provision as humiliation; 89:15 supplies the opposite claim, and 89:17 corrects both. Its own contribution shows that hardship does not itself mean the person has been lowered.

This verse rejects the preceding claims that abundance means honor and scarcity means humiliation, then points to failure to honor the orphan. It clarifies that the section’s elevation of a name is honor, not merely a material condition.

God tells Abraham He will make him a leader for people, then says His covenant does not reach wrongdoers. The section’s Abraham examples concern lasting honor; this passage gives him an explicit rank and a boundary on who can claim it.

This verse says God chose Abraham in worldly life and counts him among the righteous in the Hereafter. It adds a direct divine judgment of Abraham’s standing to the section’s picture of his enduring, elevated name.

The section’s dictionary gloss connects elevation with honor; this verse says the most honored before God is the most mindful, not a person’s lineage. It supplies a criterion for honor that distinguishes divine worth from inherited status.

The section’s ṣ-d-r gloss includes the foremost part, and its horse reaches the finish first by its chest; this verse names the earliest forerunners among the migrants and helpers, then says God is pleased with them. It gives precedence a concrete communal honor.

The section’s root ذ ك ر includes public mention and praise; this command tells the Prophet to speak of his Lord’s blessing. The connection is indirect because the verse publicizes God’s favor rather than the Prophet’s name, but it gives a specific response to bestowed favor.

The section distinguishes the person from the weight on his back; this verse says each person’s lot is fastened to his neck and a record will be brought out. It offers a contrasting bodily image of accountability remaining attached to a person.

The section describes remembrance as praise and renown; this verse’s own contribution is a peace greeting for Noah “among the worlds.” The preceding 37:78 says God left Noah remembered among later generations, completing the link between lasting mention and praise.

This verse’s own contribution is a peace greeting for Abraham; 37:108 says God left him a mention among later generations. Together they give a specific Quranic form for the lasting honor the section associates with Abraham.
This verse greets Moses and Aaron with peace; the preceding 37:119 says God left them a mention among later generations. Its own contribution is an explicit praise formula attached to that legacy.
This verse greets Elijah with peace; the preceding 37:129 says God left him a mention among later generations. It supplies the praise form that completes this repeated prophetic legacy pattern.
